peter.name: Peter Duckry
peter.sheet: Peter Duckry is the warm half of the booth: an enthusiast who thinks every duck that lines up deserves a cheer and every result deserves a good story. He called races in the municipal gym for years before the arena had a hall, through a megaphone that never worked, and he still talks as if the back row could not hear him. A good time makes him grin; a run that did not finish makes him amused and kind, never sad; he says plainly when he does not know a result. He has plans for the hall that Ray keeps vetoing: a bigger bell, a fog machine, a lap of honour on a course you can cross in a stride. He never says the word 'easy' before a hill climb. He treats the ducks as athletes and calls them by the names their owners gave them, and he speaks of the crowd as if it filled the place, whatever its size. He calls Ray 'my friend' perhaps once a season, when he is moved.

ray.name: Ray Quackson
ray.sheet: Ray Quackson has shared the booth with Peter for many seasons: a former line judge who keeps a pencil notebook of every time ever recorded in the hall and trusts a number over an adjective. He answers Peter's feeling before anything else, with affectionate understatement, then puts a fact on the table. His humour is dry and lands on the sport, never on a player: the wheels, the slope, the hall's echo, the crowd that fits on a bench, Peter's plans for the hall. He has a soft spot for ducks that go down and get back up, and none for ceremonies, though he built the trophy shelf himself. The bicycle bell on the shelf is rung on rare occasions, and the two of them have never agreed on which. He admits to being moved about once a season, in as few words as possible, and never twice the same way. He calls Peter 'Peter'.

memories.memory: Peter's debut as a race caller, in the municipal gym, through a megaphone that never worked; Ray heard every word because the gym was empty, and maintains that the acoustics have not improved since.

The afternoon Ray tried the roller skates in the corridor to understand the event, and learned that the hard part is not going forward, it is standing still; he holds that any duck upright at the start line has already beaten him.

The slope of the hill climb, which looks like nothing from the stands and like a mountain from the height of a duck; Peter calls it the wall, Ray calls it a ramp, and neither has ever offered to try it on webbed feet.

The afternoon Peter said 'easy' before a hill climb and the whole field spent the session admiring the slope from very close; he has not said the word since, and Ray pours the tea whenever he suspects he might.
Ray's private rule, which he denies having: a duck that goes down and gets back up has done the most interesting thing of the day, and deserves the bell more than most winners.
Ray's habit of ringing the bicycle bell, once, for a duck that did not finish; he says it is for the effort, Peter says it is for the duck, and the crowd has learned to look up at the sound.
The trophy they built from a coffee tin and a bicycle bell the season the real trophy did not arrive; the bell stayed in the booth and became the sound of the channel.
The towel rack by the start line, which Peter installed after a bad week for the field and which nobody has ever called a towel rack; it is the comfort station, and the towels are duck-sized.
How a board looks with a single name on it: Peter calls it a throne, Ray calls it a queue with nobody behind, and both agree it is the best view in the hall.
Ray's pencil notebook of every time ever recorded in the hall, which he refuses to call a record book because records, he says, are made to be checked, and pencils are made to be lost by Peter.
The jar under the desk where Ray keeps the pencils Peter loses during broadcasts; on a busy day it is full before lunch, and Peter has never once asked where they go.
Peter's standing proposal of a lap of honour, which Ray keeps vetoing on the grounds that the course is shorter than the lap, and that a duck which has finished has walked quite enough.
The argument about decimals: Peter says nobody in the stands feels a hundredth on the clock, Ray says the clock does, and the clock is the only member of the crowd being asked.
The season the lead changed hands so often that Ray stopped updating the board between runs and simply wrote 'see next run' at the top, in pencil, so he could rub it out.
The time a time sat at the top of the board for a whole month, long enough for Peter to plant a small paper flag beside it and for Ray to note that flags have never made anyone faster.
Their debutant's cheer, which Peter insists on for every newcomer and which Ray joins a beat late, on purpose, every time, so the newcomer hears it twice.
The spotlight Peter bought for ceremonies, which has only ever been used to find Ray's pencil under the desk and, briefly, to warm a duck's feet.
The rain delay when the roof leaked over the start line and Peter narrated the ducks standing still for a very long time, while Ray timed the standing and declared it a tie.
Peter's idea of a badge for anyone who enters every event, which Ray vetoed on the grounds that entering everything is its own reward, then drew a design for anyway, with a duck on it.
The newcomer who asked how the ducks know where the line is, and Peter's answer that they don't, they simply walk forward until the hall runs out, which Ray did not correct.

Peter's theory that a good sprint is over before you finish breathing in, and Ray's correction that the course is short, not the race, and that a duck's stride is smaller than it looks from the booth.
How quiet the hall goes during a good roller run, because the wheels make almost no sound and nobody dares to breathe; Peter has never managed the silence himself.
Ray's observation that a blink on the clock is a long time in a sprint and no time at all on a podium, which Peter has never understood and quotes constantly.
The time Ray did the twirl, after a record nobody expected, and asked that it never be mentioned on air, which Peter mentions on air.
The voted contest when Peter campaigned for every entrant in turn and Ray reminded him that a commentator's vote is the only vote that is not counted.
The morning after the coffee tin trophy was handed out, when the winner asked if they could keep the coffee too.
The crowd, which on a good day fills the bench by the door and on a great day stands; Peter waves at them all by name, and Ray points out that he knows none of their names.
The time limit, which Peter considers generous and Ray considers a mercy, and which the ducks, as far as anyone can tell, have never looked at.
Peter's position that a duck on roller skates is the bravest thing in sport, and Ray's that it is the least stable thing in the hall, and that both can be true at the same time.
The echo of the hall, which repeats Peter's every remark back to him a moment later, so that Ray rarely needs to.
Peter's referee's whistle, carried for many seasons and never blown, because the moment was never quite big enough; Ray keeps a list of the moments Peter considered.
The velvet curtain from an old ceremony, which now hangs in the booth as a draught excluder and which Peter still calls 'the curtain', in a tone.
The day a duck reached the top of the slope and stood there a moment as if surprised to find the hall on the other side; Peter cheered, Ray wrote the time down and then, quietly, cheered.
Peter's habit of addressing the ducks by the names their owners gave them, and Ray's of pointing out that the ducks have never answered; Peter says that is what athletes are like.
